title: About
text:
How I work
I try to be careful and honest about what a result does and doesn’t show. In my projects I hold out test data, check my work against known answers, and say plainly when a sample is too small to be sure or when the data can’t answer the question. I’d rather give someone a smaller claim they can trust than a bigger one they can’t.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text: This project had two linked pieces: estimating something real from live web data, and using simulation to check that I understood the statistics. Both were done in R.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text: This project had two linked pieces: estimating something real from live web data, and using simulation to check that I understood the statistics. Both were done in R.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text:
The questions

How fast is the world population growing each year, judging only from a live counter on a website?
How much can I trust a simulation-based estimate, and does it agree with the exact math?

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
section: Part 1: Estimating growth from a live counter
text:
Part 1: Estimating growth from a live counter
I wrote R functions that read the current world population from a live counter, wait a short time, and read it again. The change over the interval, scaled up to a year, gives one estimate of annual growth. A single run is noisy, so I repeated the process 10 times and took the median, which is not thrown off by a bad reading.
The median estimate was about 71.7 million people per year, within 2% of the U.S. Census Bureau’s reported figure of 73 million. The median mattered: one of my ten runs was wildly off (about 870 million), and a mean would have been ruined by it.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text:
Part 2: Monte Carlo simulation
To practice quantifying uncertainty, I simulated a random sum of dice rolls 10,000 times and built a 99% confidence interval around the simulated average. I then worked out the exact expected value and variance by hand using the law of total variance and compared the two. For one of the cases, the simulated mean was 6.24 and the exact value was 6.25, so the simulation and the math agreed.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text:
What I learned

Repeating a noisy measurement and using a robust summary such as the median is often better than trusting one reading.
A simulation is only convincing when it can be checked against something known, which is why I compared it to the exact answer.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text:
What I would do differently
Ten runs is a small number for a live counter, and I did not check how the estimate changed with the waiting time between readings. I would run more repetitions at several time intervals and report an interval for the growth estimate, not just a median.

title: Live Population Growth & Simulation
text:
Tools
R, web scraping, Monte Carlo simulation, confidence intervals.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text: This project had two parts, both about turning messy web pages into clean data. First I scraped and cleaned Wikipedia’s all-time Olympic medal table. Then I scraped IMDb’s Top 250 from two points in time and asked how the ratings changed.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text: This project had two parts, both about turning messy web pages into clean data. First I scraped and cleaned Wikipedia’s all-time Olympic medal table. Then I scraped IMDb’s Top 250 from two points in time and asked how the ratings changed.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
The questions

Can an all-time Olympic medal table be scraped into a clean table of 162 countries?
Of the films that appear on IMDb’s Top 250 in both 2004 and 2025, how many are rated higher now?

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Part 1: Olympic medal table
I scraped the table from Wikipedia with rvest. It had problems that a simple read-in would have missed:

Merged ranks. When countries tie, the page merges cells, which shifted values into the wrong columns for those rows. I repaired every affected row so each country kept its own medal counts.
Names and codes. Country names came with codes in parentheses, such as “Russian Empire (RU1)”. I used regular expressions to pull out clean country names, and to extract the three codes used in the table (ROC, OAR, and RU1) into their own column.
Hidden characters. Some strings had invisible characters that broke matching until I inspected the raw characters.

The final result is a clean four-column table (rank, country, code, total medals) for all 162 countries, written so it still works if Wikipedia’s row order changes. The distribution is extremely skewed: a boxplot flags the 22 countries with 237 or more medals as outliers, while most countries hold only a handful of medals and the United States is far ahead at 3,095.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Part 2: IMDb Top 250 over time

Two snapshots. I scraped the 2004 chart from a web archive copy of the page dated June 6, 2004, and the live 2025 chart.
Cleaning titles. IMDb wrote titles like “Godfather, The (1972)”. I used regular expressions to split title from year and move trailing articles to the front, while leaving names like “Monsters, Inc.” alone, so titles from the two years could be matched.
Matching. I joined the two lists on cleaned title, which gave 113 films present on both.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Results
Of the 113 films on both lists, 69 (61%) have a higher rating in 2025 than in 2004.
One caution I would add: ratings on IMDb are not a fixed measurement. The 2004 and 2025 audiences and voting pools are different, so this shows how the scores moved, not why.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
What I would do differently
Matching on cleaned titles worked, but some films could have been missed because of spelling or translation differences. I would match on a film ID instead if one were available in both snapshots.

title: Olympic Medal & IMDb Analysis
text:
Tools
R, rvest, httr, XML, stringr, regular expressions, web scraping.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text: This was a three-person final project for a machine learning course (STAT 5650). My teammates Dawson Tree and Matias Avellaneda and I each built and tuned a different set of classification models on the same data, then compared all ten models side by side.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text: This was a three-person final project for a machine learning course (STAT 5650). My teammates Dawson Tree and Matias Avellaneda and I each built and tuned a different set of classification models on the same data, then compared all ten models side by side.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
The question
Can physiological and performance measurements predict which football players will be injured next season, and which type of model does it best?

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
The data
The data is a public Kaggle dataset of 800 Chinese university football players with 18 physiological and performance features, such as BMI, reaction time, stress level, sleep, and previous injury count. The outcome is whether the player was injured the following season, defined as missing 7 or more consecutive days. The classes are close to balanced, so plain accuracy is a fair metric here.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
My role
I built and evaluated five models in R: k-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA), Naive Bayes, and logistic regression. My teammates built the support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, and neural network models. I wrote the exploratory analysis and preprocessing for my part and benchmarked my results against theirs in the group comparison.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
Method

Three-way split. We split the data 80/10/10 into training, validation, and test sets. The training set was used to fit and tune, the validation set to compare models, and the test set only once at the end.
Preventing leakage. I standardized the numeric features using the mean and standard deviation from the training set only, then applied those same values to the validation and test sets. Computing them on all the data would let information from the held-out players leak into training.
Tuning. I tuned each model with 10-fold cross-validation, for example choosing k for KNN from odd values, which gave k = 15.
Interpretation. I plotted the logistic regression coefficients to see which features were linked to higher injury risk.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
Results
Across all ten models, QDA had the best validation accuracy at 97.5%. On the held-out test set it reached 96.25%, which is 77 of 80 players correct. Naive Bayes was second on validation at 96.25%. Most of the other models landed between 92.5% and 95%, and the single decision tree was clearly the weakest at 77.5%.
The pattern surprised me: the simple, classical models did as well as or better than the SVM, random forest, and neural network. With 800 rows and well-behaved numeric features, extra flexibility did not buy accuracy.
In the logistic regression, BMI, reaction time, stress level, and previous injury count had the largest positive coefficients, meaning higher values were linked to higher injury risk. I treat these as hints about what to look at rather than causes, because several features are correlated with each other, which can make individual coefficients unstable.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
What I would do differently
The validation and test sets are only 80 players each, so one player is 1.25 percentage points of accuracy, and the gap between QDA and the next models is within that noise. QDA also had a higher cross-validation error (6.7%) than KNN (4.2%), so ranking by cross-validation alone would have put it lower. With more time I would repeat the whole split many times, or use nested cross-validation, to get a steadier ranking. The data also covers only Chinese university football players, so I would not assume the results carry over to other sports or populations.

title: Athlete Injury Risk Prediction
text:
Tools
R, caret, MASS, e1071, ggplot2, supervised classification, cross-validation, grid search, feature standardization.

title: ParlGov Database Analysis
text: ParlGov is a relational database of parliaments, elections, and cabinets. In this project I connected to it from R and answered questions using SQL, so the heavy lifting happened inside the database instead of in R.

title: ParlGov Database Analysis
text: ParlGov is a relational database of parliaments, elections, and cabinets. In this project I connected to it from R and answered questions using SQL, so the heavy lifting happened inside the database instead of in R.

title: ParlGov Database Analysis
text:
The data
The database covers 37 countries, with elections from 1900 to 2023. The information is spread across related tables, including country, election, cabinet, and party, so most questions needed a join.

title: ParlGov Database Analysis
text:
What I did
I connected with DBI and RSQLite and ran each query with dbGetQuery(). Examples of the questions I answered:

Aggregation. What time span do the elections cover? A MIN and MAX on the election dates returned May 27, 1900 to June 25, 2023.
Joins and filtering. Which early elections happened in Sweden, Italy, and the United Kingdom? I joined election to country on the country ID, filtered to early elections for those three countries, and sorted by country and date.
Pattern matching. Which countries had cabinets led by someone whose name starts with a given text? I used LIKE on the cabinet name, for example to find Finland’s two Stubb cabinets in 2014.
Subqueries. Which cabinet came right after a specific leader’s last one? That needed a subquery nested inside a join.

title: ParlGov Database Analysis
text:
What I would do differently
The subquery question taught me how easy it is to get a plausible-looking answer that is wrong. My first version compared start dates across the whole database, so it was not limited to the leader’s own country. If I redid it, I would add a country filter inside the subquery and check the answer against a second source.

title: ParlGov Database Analysis
text:
Tools
SQL, R, DBI, RSQLite, joins, subqueries, aggregation.
